title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Subphrenic abscesses represent localized collections of purulent material that develop in the potential space between the diaphragm and the abdominal viscera, most commonly the liver, spleen, or transverse colon. These infections typically arise as postoperative complications following abdominal surgery but may also result from trauma, perforated viscus, or inflammatory conditions such as appendicitis or diverticulitis. Pathophysiology involves contamination of the peritoneal cavity with gastrointestinal flora, followed by localization of infection beneath the diaphragm. Clinical presentation is often insidious, with nonspecific symptoms including fever, malaise, abdominal or referred shoulder pain, and respiratory complaints, contributing to delayed diagnosis and increased morbidity. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography remains the diagnostic modality of choice, enabling accurate localization and characterization of abscesses. Management focuses on timely source control through image-guided percutaneous drainage or surgical intervention, combined with targeted antimicrobial therapy to reduce the risk of sepsis and mortality.

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This educational activity equips participants with a comprehensive understanding of the evaluation and management of subphrenic abscesses in contemporary clinical practice. Learners gain proficiency in recognizing risk factors, interpreting diagnostic imaging findings, and selecting appropriate drainage strategies based on abscess anatomy and patient stability. Emphasis is placed on evidence-based antimicrobial selection and escalation of care when percutaneous management fails. Collaboration within an interprofessional healthcare team enhances patient outcomes by integrating the expertise of clinicians, surgeons, radiologists, infectious disease specialists, nurses, and pharmacists. Coordinated communication supports prompt diagnosis, efficient source control, optimized antimicrobial therapy, and vigilant monitoring for complications, ultimately improving patient safety, reducing morbidity, and supporting recovery in this high-risk population.

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Introduction
content: Described by Barlow in 1845, a subphrenic abscess occurs when pus accumulates in the space between the diaphragm and the organs beneath it, such as the liver and spleen, and can have severe clinical consequences. [1] A subphrenic abscess is characterized by abdominal pain, malaise, and fever and is accompanied by clinical and diagnostic evidence of infection. Von Volkman performed the first surgery to address a subphrenic abscess in 1879 through a combined abdominal and thoracoscopic exploration.

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Introduction
content: Frequently, a subphrenic abscess develops from abdominal surgery, trauma, or local inflammation and localizes in the spaces between the liver, intestines, and lungs, making drainage a challenging procedure. Clinical signs may often be delayed or subtle, and the diagnosis can be challenging. An aphorism developed for the subphrenic abscess is: "pus somewhere, pus nowhere else, pus under the diaphragm." [2] [3]

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Etiology
content: A subphrenic abscess forms from enteric bacteria contaminating the peritoneal cavity following surgery, trauma, or infection. Rarely, a primary subphrenic abscess develops de novo within the space between the diaphragm and the organs of the upper quadrants in the absence of an inciting incident, and this collection may be sterile. Generally, the causative organisms of a subphrenic abscess vary with surgical site and patient comorbidities. Biliary and gastric surgery accounts for more than 50% of infections in the subphrenic space.

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Etiology
content: Most infections are polymicrobial, with predominantly aerobic isolates, including Escherichia coli , Enterococcus spp , Enterobacter, and Staphylococcus aureus . The most common anaerobes are Peptostreptococcus , Bacteroides fragilis, Clostridium spp, and Prevotella . [4] Staphylococcus aureus is the most common isolate after gastric surgery, and Bacteroides fragilis and Clostridium spp are the most common after colectomy or appendectomy.

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Etiology
content: Enterococcus group D predominates after biliary surgery, Fusobacterium and Prevotella species are isolated following gastric or duodenal surgery. Multidrug-resistant Proteus mirabilis has been isolated in an immunocompetent adult. [5] Risk factors include abdominal surgery or a condition that involves significant contamination from the gastrointestinal tract, such as perforated appendicitis, gastric ulcer or diverticulitis, gastrointestinal perforation, mesenteric ischemia, trauma, empyema, and sepsis. [5] [6]

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Epidemiology
content: Subphrenic abscess is a rare diagnosis with heterogeneous pathology; therefore, statistical modeling is challenging to develop due to its infrequency and broad etiological spectrum. Primary subphrenic abscesses are rare, and their exact frequency is unknown. [7] The shifting bacteriology and epidemiology of a subphrenic abscess reflect diagnostic and therapeutic capabilities. Several decades ago, advanced appendicitis was a common etiology of a subphrenic abscess. Over time, as appendicitis treatment improved, the epidemiology shifted toward pathogens from upper gastrointestinal interventions.

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Epidemiology
content: Increasingly, traumatic injury and colon surgery comprise a greater number of subphrenic collections. [8] Right-sided abscesses account for approximately 55% of cases, left-sided 45%, and bilateral 20%. Mortality from a subphrenic abscess is as high as 30%. Recent advances in early diagnosis and nonoperative management of subphrenic abscesses have reduced incidence and improved outcomes. [9]

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Pathophysiology
content: The diaphragm, extrapleural and extraperitoneal, separates the thoracic and abdominal cavities and is covered by pleura and peritoneum. The pleura attaches posteriorly to the 12th rib, laterally to the tenth rib, and anteriorly to the eighth rib, and is in proximity to a subphrenic abscess. A subphrenic abscess may extend into the pleural spaces directly or hematogenously, and can lead to a secondary pulmonary abscess.

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Pathophysiology
content: Inflammatory changes and increased capillary permeability can facilitate the formation of a pleural effusion. The subphrenic space is partially divided by the broad peritoneal folding of the falciform ligament. The peri-diaphragmatic area above the liver is often affected by extraperitoneal infections like retrocecal or retroperitoneal appendicitis, a renal abscess, or perforation of the retroperitoneal portion of the duodenum.

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Pathophysiology
content: The intraperitoneal space above the liver, limited medially by the falciform ligament, is a common location for pyogenic and amebic abscesses, and processes that originate inferiorly, such as appendicitis or pelvic infections that ascend through the paracolic gutter. The intraperitoneal space below the liver, Morrison pouch, communicates with the right paracolic gutter and often harbors infections from perforated ulcers and gallbladder empyema. The perisplenic space may become infected by a gastric perforation, malignant seeding from colon, gastric, pancreatic, or ovarian primaries, bacteria from splenectomy or colectomy, or other routes.

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Pathophysiology
content: The lesser sac sits behind the stomach and the lesser omentum, and anterior to the pancreas and transverse mesocolon. The left kidney forms the superior margin, and the transverse colon forms the floor. Enclosed on the sides by the portal triad and the gastrosplenic ligament. Infection in this area is usually caused by perforation of the posterior wall of the stomach. [10]

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Histopathology
content: Histopathology of a subphrenic abscess varies by etiology, but in general, it contains purulent material enclosed by an inflammatory rind. Microscopically, the material consists of a mixture of inflammatory cells, including CD3-, CD20-, and PAX5-positive lymphocytes; CD38-positive plasma cells; CD68-positive macrophages; and CD15-positive granulocytes. The fibrous and hyalinized stroma contains fibroblasts and capillaries. [5] [11] [12] [13]

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- History and Physical
content: A person with a subphrenic abscess typically presents with generalized symptoms, including fever, rigors, costal vertebral angle tenderness, shoulder pain, abdominal pain, and malaise. They may have experienced recent surgery or trauma that involved an open viscus or uncontained intrabdominal contamination. A delay in diagnosis, bowel ischemia, and immunosuppression increase the risk of an abscess. Due to the location, pulmonary symptoms can be the chief presenting complaint, including dyspnea, hiccup, and cough. Those who present in a delayed fashion may have systemic inflammatory response syndrome and sepsis, with tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria, and possibly multiorgan failure. [14] [15] [16]

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Evaluation
content: Laboratory and radiographic assessments aid in diagnosing a subphrenic abscess. Blood tests reveal leukocytosis with neutrophilia and an elevated sedimentation rate. Blood cultures, aspirate culture, and Gram stains will demonstrate polymicrobial pathogens. An x-ray will often rule out an elevated hemidiaphragm, atelectasis, pleural effusion, or consolidation.

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Evaluation
content: Further, gas may be detected below the diaphragm. Computed tomography (CT) is the best imaging modality for a left upper quadrant process, and will reveal the air-fluid level with wall enhancement. An abscess source may be identified during assessment of the abdominal and pelvic spaces. Ultrasound also demonstrates a heterogeneous fluid collection containing gas and debris and is frequently used to diagnose right-sided collections.

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Evaluation
content: Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and an indium-111-labeled leukocyte scan may be helpful for an occult intra-abdominal or subphrenic abscess. MR enterography is the investigation of choice in patients with active inflammatory bowel disease and possible abscess. Blood gas analysis may initially reveal respiratory alkalosis due to hyperventilation, which may progress to metabolic acidosis if left untreated. [14] [17] In pregnant patients with suspected acute intra-abdominal abscess, ultrasound or MRI can be considered as the initial diagnostic imaging modality. [18]

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Treatment / Management
content: Initial management of a subphrenic abscess consists of resuscitation as indicated. Supportive and therapeutic care includes broad-spectrum antibiotics, fluid replenishment, mechanical and pharmacologic adjuncts for any decrement in oxygenation. Patients who are hypoxic, hemodynamically unstable, or obtunded may require mechanical ventilation and pharmacologic hemodynamic support until their condition stabilizes. Concurrently, the interdisciplinary team collaborates on the safest and most effective route of source control. Factors associated with poor clinical outcomes include: Delayed intervention APACHE II score greater than 15 Advanced age Multiple comorbidities Organ dysfunction Hypoalbuminemia Poor nutritional status Diffuse peritonitis Incomplete debridement or drainage Malignancy

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Treatment / Management
content: If the collection is accessible percutaneously, CT-guided aspiration and drain placement are effective and can be performed without general anesthesia. Complex collections may require multiple drains or surgical drainage. A subphrenic abscess may be a finding amidst an open abdomen resulting from trauma or sepsis and is treated during sequential scheduled washouts. Additional drainage options, depending on the precise abscess location, include endoscopic transgastric drainage. [3] [19] [20]

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Treatment / Management
content: Early administration of antibiotics improves outcomes. Either combination regimens or single broad-spectrum antibiotics may be used. For mild-to-moderate community-acquired infections, suitable single agents include ticarcillin-clavulanate, cefoxitin, ertapenem, moxifloxacin, or tigecycline; combinations such as metronidazole with cefazolin, cefuroxime, ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, levofloxacin, or ciprofloxacin are also effective. For severe community-acquired infections, empiric regimens should provide broad Gram-negative coverage. Effective antimicrobials include meropenem, imipenem-cilastatin, doripenem, piperacillin-tazobactam, or ciprofloxacin/levofloxacin with metronidazole, or ceftazidime/cefepime with metronidazole.

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Treatment / Management
content: For healthcare-associated infections, therapy is guided by local resistance patterns; these infections may require multidrug regimens with expanded Gram-negative coverage such as meropenem, imipenem-cilastatin, doripenem, piperacillin-tazobactam, or ceftazidime/cefepime plus metronidazole. In cases involving multidrug-resistant organisms, aminoglycosides or colistin may be necessary. [6] In immunosuppressed individuals, antifungal agents active against Candida may be indicated. Azoles are preferred when the patient is stable, and cultures are sensitive to azoles. In those who are critically ill, and if nonalbicans Candida is noted, echinocandins like anidulafungin are the drug of choice. [21] Antibiotic duration depends on the speciation and extent of infection. The Surgical Infection Society guidelines recommend 96 hours for well-controlled collections and 5 to 7 days for those without drainage procedures. [22]

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Treatment / Management
content: Percutaneous CT-guided drainage is considered the gold standard for managing subphrenic abscesses, offering a high success rate with minimal invasiveness. A needle is advanced under the costal margin, often using fluoroscopy, to dilate the track and place a catheter into the collection. This approach avoids the need for general anesthesia, particularly advantageous in elderly or critically ill individuals with multiple comorbidities, and reduces postoperative wound complications and hospital stay.

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Treatment / Management
content: Drainage serves both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes, allowing aspiration for microbiologic evaluation while providing effective source control. In those who are unstable or at high risk, percutaneous drainage can also serve as a bridge to definitive surgery, helping stabilize the patient by controlling sepsis. Persistent drainage after aspiration may indicate an enteric fistula or another leak, which contrast-enhanced CT can confirm.

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Treatment / Management
content: Potential complications of image-guided drainage include bleeding, injury to adjacent organs, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, and mediastinitis. Endoscopic ultrasound–guided transgastric or transesophageal drainage provides real-time visualization of the abscess cavity and Doppler imaging to identify and avoid vascular structures, with excellent clinical outcomes. [19] In cases where a subphrenic abscess cannot be completely drained with CT-guided aspiration and drain placement, instillation of fibrinolytic agents such as tissue plasminogen activator through the drain may enhance drainage by dissolving fibrinous septations within the abscess cavity. This approach has been shown to result in clinical improvement in select patients who are poor surgical candidates or in whom percutaneous drainage is incomplete. [23]

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Treatment / Management
content: When percutaneous or endoscopic drainage fails, surgical intervention is necessary and performed via either a laparoscopic or open approach. Laparoscopic drainage reduces postoperative pain and provides direct visualization. An open surgical approach is required if laparoscopy is not feasible; however, it can be technically challenging due to bowel adhesions, distorted anatomy, and friable tissues.

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Treatment / Management
content: Video-assisted thoracic trans-disphragmatic approaches have also been described, and some institutions now standardize the use of an intercostal approach when indicated for more direct access. [24] In cases involving abdominal compartment syndrome or multi-trauma, an open abdomen may be necessary. This technique uses temporary abdominal closure methods, such as vacuum-assisted dressings, to control contamination during sequential scheduled returns to the operating room in critically ill individuals. [22] [24]

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Several conditions can present with clinical features similar to those of a subphrenic abscess, including fever, abdominal pain, and elevated inflammatory markers, such as inflammatory bowel disease, prolonged ileus, postoperative atelectasis, pneumonia, or lung abscess. Differential diagnosis also includes hepatic abscess, subphrenic hematoma, empyema, pancreatic abscess or pseudocyst, gallbladder empyema or perforation, perinephric abscess, and, less commonly, diaphragmatic or subcostal tumors or a congenital cyst. Radiographic mimics include intraluminal gas, gastric outlet obstruction, and post-operative air following intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal surgery. Careful clinical correlation with laboratory evaluation and cross-sectional imaging is crucial for distinguishing these entities and guiding appropriate management. [25] [26]
contents: Subphrenic Abscess -- Differential Diagnosis. Several conditions can present with clinical features similar to those of a subphrenic abscess, including fever, abdominal pain, and elevated inflammatory markers, such as inflammatory bowel disease, prolonged ileus, postoperative atelectasis, pneumonia, or lung abscess. Differential diagnosis also includes hepatic abscess, subphrenic hematoma, empyema, pancreatic abscess or pseudocyst, gallbladder empyema or perforation, perinephric abscess, and, less commonly, diaphragmatic or subcostal tumors or a congenital cyst. Radiographic mimics include intraluminal gas, gastric outlet obstruction, and post-operative air following intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal surgery. Careful clinical correlation with laboratory evaluation and cross-sectional imaging is crucial for distinguishing these entities and guiding appropriate management. [25] [26]

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Surgical Oncology
content: In patients who undergo gastrectomy for gastric cancer, the incidence of a subphrenic abscess can be as high as 4%, most often following a total gastrectomy, secondary to an anastomotic leak. [27]

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis for patients with subdiaphragmatic abscesses has improved markedly in recent decades with more rapid diagnosis and minimally invasive drainage techniques. The use of computed tomography for diagnosis and image-guided drainage has significantly reduced morbidity and mortality. Outcomes depend on several factors, including the underlying etiology, comorbidities, time to treatment, and the extent of infection.

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Prognosis
content: Multiorgan failure remains the primary cause of death, particularly in cases complicated by delayed source control. Early recognition, prompt resuscitation, targeted antimicrobial therapy, and effective drainage have collectively reduced mortality from 40% to 60% to approximately 18% to 30%. With comprehensive, interdisciplinary management and advances in critical care, most patients now recover fully with minimal long-term sequelae. [28] [29]

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Complications
content: A subphrenic abscess can lead to local and systemic complications, with any delay in diagnosis exacerbating these complications. Intra-abdominal complications include generalized peritonitis, enteric fistulae, and ileus. Thoracic complications include pleurisy, pleural effusion, empyema, lung abscess, or bronchial fistula. Infection may progress to a multi-located or diffuse process or sepsis. Complications from intervention include injury to vessels or organs and pneumothorax. [8] [29]

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: Most patients with a subphrenic abscess recover without residual effects. However, patients with a prolonged intensive care course experience deconditioning and benefit from early physical, occupational, and speech therapy to restore strength, mobility, and overall functional status. Respiratory therapy, including deep breathing exercises and early mobilization, plays a crucial role in recovery.

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Consultations
content: Management of subphrenic abscesses often requires an interprofessional team that may include an emergency clinician, radiologist, surgeon, intensivist, microbiologist, and infectious disease specialist. Each member contributes unique expertise, prompt diagnosis and stabilization in the emergency setting, radiology-guided imaging and drainage, surgical intervention when needed, critical care support, and targeted antimicrobial management to ensure timely, coordinated, and effective patient care.

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Subphrenic abscesses may arise as complications of conditions such as cholecystitis, diverticulitis, or appendicitis, and are more likely in patients with risk factors like recent abdominal surgery, diabetes, or inflammatory bowel disease. Education is essential for early recognition and intervention. Patients should be counseled regarding symptoms, including fever, abdominal or shoulder pain, chest discomfort, and loss of appetite. Because outcomes depend on the underlying cause and timeliness of treatment, those with recent intra-abdominal surgery should be advised to seek immediate medical evaluation if these symptoms occur.

title: Subphrenic Abscess -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: A subphrenic abscess often presents with vague symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and leukocytosis, requiring imaging for accurate diagnosis. Optimal management requires an interprofessional team approach that involves surgeons, radiologists, intensivists, microbiologists, infectious disease specialists, nurses, and pharmacists. Clear communication among all members ensures rapid diagnosis, recognition of complications, coordinated treatment, and improved outcomes. This collaborative, patient-centered approach enhances both safety and recovery.
